recipe.history:
Coleslaw — the creamy, mayonnaise-dressed shredded cabbage salad that has become synonymous with American barbecue and picnics — traces its name to the Dutch koolsla, meaning cabbage salad, brought to America by Dutch settlers in New Amsterdam (present-day New York) in the seventeenth century. Cabbage itself is one of humanity's oldest cultivated vegetables, domesticated from wild Brassica oleracea along the Atlantic coast of Europe, and has been a staple of Northern European, Eastern European, and Asian diets for millennia precisely because it keeps well through winter. The Dutch version was a simple preparation of shredded raw cabbage dressed with a warm bacon fat and vinegar dressing — quite different from the mayonnaise-based preparation that became dominant after Hellmann's mayonnaise began mass production in New York in the early twentieth century. The vinegar slaw tradition, meanwhile, is the older and in some ways truer form: it predates mayonnaise, relies on vinegar's natural preservative qualities, and remains the preferred style in North Carolina barbecue culture, where a bright, acidic vinegar slaw is served not as a side but as a topping inside pulled pork sandwiches and burgers — placed between the meat and the bun to provide crunchy, acidic contrast to the rich fat.

Coleslaw on burgers reflects the American instinct to add crunch and acid to a composition that is otherwise all richness. The hamburger — bread, beef, fat-based sauces — is in its basic form a study in soft, yielding textures and savory, umami flavors. Coleslaw intervenes with crunch, brightness, and freshness, providing structural and flavor contrast. California's burger culture in the 1960s and 1970s embraced coleslaw toppings enthusiastically, and the combination of creamy slaw with a juicy patty became a defining element of West Coast burger identity. The double-slaw approach — layering creamy mayo-dressed coleslaw and sharp vinegar-dressed coleslaw in the same burger — multiplies this contrast: you get the richness and sweetness of the creamy layer alongside the pure acid brightness of the vinegar layer, two different philosophies of the same ingredient operating simultaneously, creating a harmony that neither alone can achieve.

I grew up eating coleslaw at every summer cookout and I was always vaguely bored by it until I was in my twenties and I ate a pulled pork sandwich in a small roadside place in North Carolina where the slaw was the point, not the garnish. It was a vinegar slaw — no mayo, just cider vinegar, a little sugar, celery seed, and shredded green cabbage — and it was inside the bun with the pork, soaking into the bread, cutting through the pork fat with a brightness that made every bite simultaneously rich and clean. I drove back to my kitchen that night and made both versions — the creamy one I had always eaten and the vinegar one I had just discovered — and I put them side by side and ate them with a fork, studying the difference. Then I made a burger and put both on it, and it was, to my enormous surprise, more correct than either alone. The dreamy, velvet, Los Angeles quality of this burger — its Slaw Slaw Land identity — comes from that sense of two complementary visions existing together.

In a burger this textured — two slaws, a toasted bun, sauce — the patty must be medium rare. The entire design of this burger hinges on contrast: creamy against sharp, soft against crunchy, rich against bright. Medium rare provides a third layer of contrast: a yielding, rosy, juicy interior against the crisp crust and the snapping crunch of the slaws. A well-done patty collapses that contrast. It is dry, it is uniform in texture, and it has nothing to offer the slaws except a surface. The medium-rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit is the fulcrum around which every other element balances. Pull it early. Rest it properly. Let the meat be what it wants to be.
ingredients: 4 large eggs (3 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
2 cups green cabbage, very finely shredded
Salt and white pepper to taste
2 cups green cabbage, very finely shredded
1/2 medium red onion, very thinly sliced
instructions: 1. Make the vinegar slaw first (it benefits from time): Toss shredded cabbages and red onion in a large bowl. Whisk together apple cider vinegar, sugar, celery seed, red pepper flakes, salt, and neutral oil in a small bowl until sugar dissolves. Pour over cabbage and toss thoroughly. Refrigerate at least 1 hour, tossing occasionally. Drain excess liquid before using.

2. Make the creamy coleslaw: Combine green cabbage, purple cabbage, and carrot in a bowl. In a separate small bowl, whisk together mayonnaise, apple cider vinegar, sugar, celery seed, Dijon mustard, salt, and white pepper. Pour dressing over cabbage and toss until fully coated. Taste and adjust seasoning. Refrigerate at least 30 minutes before serving.

3. Make the brioche buns: Combine warm milk, warm water, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add sugar, salt, and 3 eggs. Add flour one cup at a time with the dough hook on low. Increase to medium speed, add butter cube by cube, and knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and refrigerate 8 hours or overnight.

4. Divide dough into 4 equal portions. Shape into tight balls. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover loosely and proof at room temperature 1.5 to 2 hours. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush with egg wash, sprinkle with sesame seeds, and bake 16 to 18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.

5. Make the burger sauce: Whisk together mayonnaise, ketchup, relish, mustard, smoked paprika, garlic powder, and apple cider vinegar until smooth. Season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

6. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions. Shape into 4-inch patties, 3/4-inch thick, with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides generously with salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Refrigerate 15 minutes.

7. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat and lightly oil the surface. Sear patties dimple-side up, undisturbed, for 3 minutes. Flip once, lay a slice of American cheese on each patty, and cook 2 to 3 more minutes until internal temperature reaches 130 to 135°F. Remove from heat, tent with foil, and rest 3 minutes.
8. Split buns and toast cut-side down in butter in the skillet over medium heat until golden, about 90 seconds.

9. Assemble the burgers: Spread burger sauce generously on both cut sides of the bun. Place the rested patty with melted cheese on the bottom bun. Layer a generous mound of creamy coleslaw directly on top of the cheese. Add a smaller mound of the drained vinegar slaw on top of the creamy slaw. Close with the top bun. Serve immediately — the double slaw is best eaten right away while the textures are distinct.
